questions.question: Q1. In a standard servo-PWM throttle signal, which property of the signal encodes the throttle command?

answers.a: The voltage amplitude of the pulse
answers.b: The width (duration) of the high pulse
answers.d: The rise time of the pulse edge

explanations.a: Incorrect — the logic voltage (e.g. 3.3 V or 5 V) is fixed; it does not carry the command.
explanations.b: Correct — the throttle is encoded in the pulse WIDTH (1000 us = 0%, 2000 us = 100%), independent of voltage or frequency.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the refresh frequency sets how often a command is sent (latency), not the command value.
explanations.d: Incorrect — edge rise time is a signal-integrity property, not the command.

questions.question: Q2. What are the conventional minimum and maximum throttle pulse widths for a calibrated RC ESC?

explanations.a: Incorrect — a 0 us pulse is no signal at all.
explanations.b: Incorrect — these are not the standard servo endpoints.
explanations.c: Correct — the RC servo standard maps 1000 us to 0% throttle and 2000 us to 100% throttle, a 1000 us active band.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 5000 us exceeds even a 50 Hz frame budget used for control.

questions.question: Q3. What is the purpose of the arming dead-band at the bottom of the throttle range?

answers.a: To increase the maximum thrust available
answers.b: To prevent signal jitter or trim offsets from spinning the propeller while armed at idle
answers.c: To reduce the ESC's power consumption at full throttle

explanations.a: Incorrect — the dead-band only affects the bottom of the range, not maximum thrust.
explanations.b: Correct — the dead-band (1000-1050 us = 0%) forces a guaranteed zero-spin idle so noise or trim cannot creep the rotor on an armed aircraft.
explanations.c: Incorrect — it is a safety gate on the idle command, unrelated to full-throttle power.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the dead-band has nothing to do with refresh frequency.

questions.question: Q4. Why must each ESC be calibrated to the transmitter's throttle endpoints?

answers.a: To increase the motor's top speed
answers.b: So every ESC maps the same stick position to the same throttle, with full stick travel spanning 0-100%
answers.c: To lower the ESC's conduction resistance
answers.d: To raise the PWM refresh frequency

explanations.a: Incorrect — calibration sets the command mapping, not the motor's top speed.
explanations.b: Correct — calibration teaches each ESC which pulse widths mean 0% and 100%, so all motors respond identically to the same stick and the full stick travel maps to the full 0-100% range. Comparing this ideal map to the real response is the Expected-vs-Obtained exercise.
explanations.c: Incorrect — calibration does not change the MOSFET conduction resistance.
explanations.d: Incorrect — calibration is independent of the refresh frequency.

questions.question: Q5. Does raising the PWM refresh frequency from 50 Hz to 400 Hz make the throttle control finer (more steps)?

answers.a: Yes, it multiplies the number of throttle steps by 8
answers.b: No — resolution (number of steps) is set by the timer tick; higher frequency only lowers latency
answers.c: Yes, higher frequency always means finer resolution
answers.d: No — higher frequency actually reduces the number of steps

explanations.a: Incorrect — the step count does not scale with refresh frequency.
explanations.b: Correct — the number of steps depends on the timer tick and pulse band (1000 steps at 1 us). Higher frequency reduces command latency (20 ms to 2.5 ms), not resolution.
explanations.c: Incorrect — this is the common misconception the experiment corrects.
explanations.d: Incorrect — resolution is unchanged, not reduced.

questions.question: Q6. What is the governing equation for the conduction power loss dissipated by an ESC's MOSFETs?

explanations.a: Incorrect — V*I is the power delivered to the load, not the loss inside the ESC.
explanations.b: Correct — conduction loss is P = I^2 * R_ESC, the current squared times the MOSFET on-resistance.
explanations.c: Incorrect — this is dimensionally and physically wrong for power dissipation.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that is capacitive switching loss, a separate (smaller) term not used in this sub-calculation.

questions.question: Q7. Above what per-ESC conduction loss does this experiment flag that a heatsink (active cooling) is required?

explanations.a: Incorrect — 0.5 W is easily handled by passive convection.
explanations.b: Incorrect — 1 W is below the flagged threshold.
explanations.c: Correct — the experiment uses a 2 W per-ESC dissipation threshold above which a heatsink is recommended.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 10 W would already be a severe overheating condition, far above the decision threshold.

questions.question: Q8. How does the conduction resistance of the ESC's MOSFET channel change as its temperature rises?

answers.d: It drops to zero above 80 degC

explanations.a: Incorrect — a silicon power MOSFET has a positive, not negative, Rds(on) temperature coefficient.
explanations.b: Incorrect — assuming constant R is the simplification the experiment corrects.
explanations.c: Correct — MOSFET Rds(on) rises with temperature (alpha ~ 0.006 /degC, climbing to ~1.45x by 100 degC), so R(T) = R25*(1 + alpha*(T-25)); the ESC dissipates more heat when hot.
explanations.d: Incorrect — resistance does not vanish; it keeps increasing with temperature.

questions.question: Q9. What is the worst-case command latency of a 50 Hz PWM signal?

explanations.a: Incorrect — 2 ms corresponds to a 500 Hz signal.
explanations.b: Incorrect — 2.5 ms corresponds to a 400 Hz signal.
explanations.d: Correct — latency = 1/f = 1/50 = 0.02 s = 20 ms, the long refresh period of legacy 50 Hz PWM; the simulator shows the response lagging the command by this much.

questions.question: Q10. How does a digital protocol like DShot encode throttle, compared to analog PWM?

answers.a: As an analog pulse width that still needs endpoint calibration
answers.b: As a digital integer value (11-bit, ~2000 levels) requiring no endpoint calibration or dead-band
answers.c: As a varying voltage level on the signal wire
answers.d: As the frequency of the signal

explanations.a: Incorrect — DShot is digital and needs no analog calibration.
explanations.b: Correct — DShot sends an 11-bit throttle word (2048 codes, ~2000 usable) plus a checksum; the endpoints are exact integers, so no calibration or dead-band is needed.
explanations.c: Incorrect — DShot is a clocked digital bitstream, not an analog voltage level.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the throttle is in the data word, not the signal frequency.
